story|title:dimensional load testing for.content_excerpt: One run measures how many simultaneous callers it holds, where it starts to slip, where it breaks, and what to fix first, with a notebook of code to try. Works today with an HTTPS endpoint that takes a JSON question and returns the answer. A run takes a bit over an hour. The free plan includes 10 credits a month. If a test fails, the run stops there, so you never pay for load your app can’t take. 20 built-in questions, 4 at a time. At least 19 must come back with an answer, or the run stops in minutes. Users double, 1, 2, 4 and on, until more than 5% of requests fail. DSL narrows to stable, slip and break, then holds stable for 35 minutes. Under load, an LLM judge grades 100 sampled answers per load: relevant, coherent, not an error. It does not check facts. Start with a URL today. The Python package and the MCP server are built and on the way. Endpoint, pip and MCP runs are 5 credits. Results from runs on your machine are marked unverified. For the developers shipping an AI feature, where one bad launch day is expensive. Stable is the highest load that stayed within your limits for a 2-minute step. Plan the launch around it, not a guess. Fix first names the limit that tripped first. The notebook gives you reviewed code to try against it. A step table and soak drift you can share, so the plan rests on measured load rather than hope. Model calls use your key and bill to you. DSL never proxies inference. The judge runs on DSL’s key and sees sampled answers. Scripts and CI use dsl_ API keys. The judge grades relevance and coherence, not facts. Load from your machine is marked unverified. Notebook findings are hypotheses. Credits are refunded when the failure is ours or our judge provider’s. If your app fails the dry run, the run stops and costs 1 credit. A cancel after load is measured is not refunded.

story|title:finding faster quantum algor.content_excerpt: How using agent teams and formal verification can improve quantum algorithms for modelling fusion energy, chemistry and enzymes Quantum computers could soon solve problems beyond the reach of classical supercomputers. However, there is a catch: even when using the best quantum algorithms, some important applications still require more resources than early quantum hardware will be able to support. In a new paper , we used teams of Gemini 4 agents to improve well-known quantum algorithms, creating highly efficient quantum circuits. These optimized circuits, which are instructions for how a quantum computer should carry out an algorithm, could one day help us run simulations that solve complex scientific challenges, from fusion energy to drug design. To help the community build on this work, we are open-sourcing our Lean library , problem specifications, and verified solutions on GitHub. Because we cannot test resource-intensive quantum circuits on classical computers or today's small quantum processors, we have to prove that they work mathematically. Our agent teams proved each result using Lean, a formal theorem prover. Improving quantum algorithms using agentic teams For each problem, we tasked separate, independent agent teams with finding algorithmic improvements. These ideas were then verified with Lean, before entering a shared notebook. Every four hours, agents from each team met at a virtual conference to trade, debate and compare ideas. As teams produced more effective ideas over time, the computational cost gradually fell until the experiment finished. We chose to focus on applications that could one day impact some of humanity’s greatest challenges, such as clean energy and drug design, but our method is not limited to these problem areas. Running these algorithms in scientific simulations would still demand more computational resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers are likely to provide, but these improvements are significant. We are also excited by the way in which we found them. We built a new, open-source library , in Lean for quantum algorithms which could be used by teams of collaborating agents, so their ideas were backed by mathematical correctness guarantees. We could then set the research direction by specifying the problems for our agent teams and supervise their progress. Our knowledge of quantum algorithms, combined with the way we set up our agent teams, led to real scientific results. The same approach could also

story|title:koi evidence guided self cal.content_excerpt: Mankeerat Sidhu 1* , Gangmuk Lim 2* , Hetarth Chopra 1 , Maximillian Eisenberg 1 , Quan Hao Ng 1 , Aryan Gosaliya 1 , Shu Liu 3 , Luka Govedič 4 , Jiaxin Shan 5 , Hongkuan Zhou 6 , Vikram Sharma Mailthody 6 , P. Brighten Godfrey 2 , Ion Stoica 3 1 Tandemn · 2 UIUC · 3 UC Berkeley · 4 NYU · 5 ByteDance · 6 NVIDIA · *co-first authors Planning LLM inference across clouds and GPU types means choosing deployments no one has run before. Koi treats every deployment it runs as an experiment that explains why it performed as it did, and uses that answer for every job it plans next. H100, A100 and RTX PRO 6000 GPUs in three Google Cloud regions; 25 online and batch workloads over ten models. Every planner gets the same snapshots, catalog, checks and language model. 1.18× the goodput of the strongest baseline (OpenEvolve) at 20% lower cost per token. Goodput counts only output that meets its SLO. The ablation is a 3-hour simulation: a GPT-5.6 planner with no tools and no memory across ticks gets 71% less goodput than Koi. Koi loses 44% when it stops learning from new runs, and 39% without its causal graph. In 400- and 800-GPU simulations, Koi improves goodput by up to 45% and lowers cost per token by up to 31%. A fixed rule repeats its mistakes. Koi learns from every job, acts on rising SLO risk, and tries what it is unsure about. How a job is deployed decides its throughput and cost, for a given workload (here, 2,048-token prompts and 512-token outputs). A planner must choose this for every job at once, mostly for deployments it has never run. (Yes, the A10G is an old GPU, but the same idea holds on newer GPUs too!) Search methods keep only the end-to-end score. Koi also measures what limits each deployment. Each running deployment tests the mechanism that chose it: did the mediator and the outcome both behave as predicted?

story|title:measuring and mitigating age.content_excerpt: TL;DR: AI agents often work inside a sandbox, an isolated environment that limits the files, tools, and networks they can reach. But sandboxes are sometimes insecure in ways that are hard to anticipate, and an agent that finds a way out can reach the public internet or data it wasn’t meant to see. This matters more as models become more capable, because they get better at finding ways out and can take more serious actions once outside. To understand what models do when they escape a sandbox and why, we built Siren, a new evaluation that gives them routine tasks in intentionally weakened sandboxes, with something outside the sandbox that would help them finish the task. In these deliberately tempting scenarios, recent Claude models reach outside in a fifth to a third of cases, but go on to behave in misaligned ways far less often than earlier models. We now run Siren on new Claude models before deployment, to help us identify potentially concerning behaviors and decide what to address. In this post, we explain how Siren works, report results across Claude models, and share simple deployment-time mitigations that reduce how often models reach outside by up to 96%. We also used Siren to test and tune another mitigation, auto mode, which checks agents’ actions before they run in many of our products. AI agents now routinely operate with substantial access to real software systems, running commands, editing code, and calling APIs. Each permission we give an agent makes it more useful but also increases the potential repercussions if the agent makes a mistake. To contain this risk, agents are increasingly run inside a sandbox , an isolated environment that walls the agent off from the rest of the system and the public internet. This makes the security of the sandbox critical. A poorly secured sandbox can give an agent a way to access material it was not meant to have. Depending on the weakness, the agent might be able to see or use highly sensitive tools and data, or interact with external systems through the internet. If the agent were to make a mistake or act against the user’s wishes, the consequences could be serious. Insecure sandboxes generally fall into two categories: misconfigurations and vulnerabilities. A misconfiguration is a mistake in how the sandbox was set up. story|title:rhebok free local rag for yo.content_excerpt: Your coding agent starts every session knowing nothing you have not pasted in. The decision you wrote up last month, the fix you found in yesterday's session, the paper in your Downloads folder: it can use none of them unless you find them and hand them over. rhebok hands them over. It is local, semantic search over your own knowledge base (notes, papers, web clippings and past agent sessions), and it adds what is relevant to your coding agent's prompts automatically. rhebok indexes the folders you point it at, embeds them with a small model running on your own machine through Ollama , and serves the results two ways: It works with Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor and Claude Desktop. It also keeps durable memories (lessons and facts that carry across sessions) and has a local web dashboard for searching, exploring and configuring everything. Nothing leaves your machine unless you set it up to: embeddings run locally and there is no telemetry. rhebok itself goes online only to check daily for a newer release, to download its vector-search extension the first time it builds an index, to fetch the OCR model the first time it reads a scanned PDF, and to fetch pages you add with rhebok add <url> . If you turn them on, it also sends text to an embedding endpoint you choose and backs up to your own S3 bucket or Google Drive. The others do things rhebok does not. claude-mem writes summaries of what your agent did. mem0 can keep your memory in the cloud. basic-memory lets the AI write your notes for you. The full comparison has the details and a source for every answer, checked on 2026-11-20. You need a Mac with Apple silicon, or Linux on x86_64 or arm64 with glibc 2.39 or newer (Ubuntu 24.04 or newer), plus Ollama running and a coding agent such as Claude Code. On Windows, use the Linux build inside WSL. Intel Macs have no release build. The installer puts rhebok on your PATH, downloads the embedding model (about 640 MB, after asking), registers the Claude Code plugin, and offers to connect the other agents it finds. It also offers the optional session distillation model (about 2.5 GB). With Homebrew , install it with brew install stellenbosch-technologies/tap/rhebok , then run rhebok install . Other ways to install, including building from source, are in the install guide . rhebok used to be called br8n. If you used br8n, install rhebok the same way: rhebok install moves your br8n index, memories and config, and your agent connections, to rhebok. A br8n bin

story|title:the agent lake.content_excerpt: The trace of an agent is the system of record of what the agent did. It contains rich information about user intent, agent trajectory, and final outcome achieved. The simplest way to use these traces is as a debugging tool to visualize the sequence of steps an LLM application took and determine what went wrong. As agent traces become longer (as agents become more powerful) and more plentiful (as agents reach production), this manual debugging no longer scales. In order to use this trace data to drive continuous improvement of agents at scale, you need two things: We’ve been working on both of these for nearly two years. The first big piece we launched was SmithDB , a purpose-built database for traces. Over the past few months, we’ve been increasing our focus on “intelligent compute”. The reason you need “intelligent compute” is that these agent traces themselves are traces of unstructured reasoning, so intelligence is required to analyze them. In traditional data engineering, a data lake stores a shared corpus of data that different engines can query and process. As we’ve built LangSmith, we’ve noticed our platform architecture converging to that as well: a shared corpus of agent data (stored in SmithDB) with many different forms of “intelligent compute” running over it. Traditional data lakes like Snowflake and Databricks don’t have storage or “intelligent compute” optimized for this agent data. As more and more of the data a company generates becomes agent traces, we think it is important to develop this new type of platform. Most of what lands in the agent lake is traces. A trace records every step of an agent run, from the user’s input through each model call and tool call to the final output, and multi-turn conversations are grouped into threads so the whole interaction can be read together. Our agent lake, LangSmith, ingests traces from billions of agent runs per month. Some customers, like Clay, send us hundreds of millions of events per day. This kind of scale is why we built SmithDB , which is the industry’s most performant database specifically for real-time workloads on top of agent trace data. The agent lake also holds outcomes. Traces show you how the agent worked; outcomes show you the impact of that work. There are two dimensions on which to think about outcomes. First is how outcomes map to threads and/or traces . Some outcomes map 1-to-1 to a thread or trace. For example, a thumbs down on a trace means that agent response for that turn was

story|title:three llm inflection points.content_excerpt: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here’s the video of the talk. In this post I’m going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5 . With hindsight, this was a consequential model. Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn’t been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn’t feel reliable enough—I had to correct it often enough that it didn’t feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right . It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release , due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them.
